title: Question 8
stem:
A circuit incorporating an ideal operational amplifier (op-amp) is shown in Fig. 8.1.
{{figure:figure_8_1}}
The supply to the op-amp is $+9\text{ V}/-9\text{ V}$.
The output of the amplifier is measured using a voltmeter having a range $0-5.0\text{ V}$.
A switch enables the inverting input to the op-amp to be connected to either resistor $R_A$ or resistor $R_B$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
A positive potential $+V_{IN}$ is applied to the input to the circuit.
On Fig. 8.1, mark with the letter P the positive connection of the voltmeter such that the voltmeter shows a positive reading.

markscheme_points.text: P shown between earth symbol and voltmeter

hints: Hint 1: Think about the sign of the output when a positive voltage goes into the inverting (-) input, and remember a voltmeter reads positive when its positive terminal is at higher potential than its negative terminal.
parts.proper_answer: Mark P on the lower (earthed) lead of the voltmeter. The inverting amplifier gives a negative output, so the earth at $0\text{ V}$ must go to the positive terminal.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the Inverting Amplifier**
You are looking at an inverting amplifier because the input signal goes through $R_A$ or $R_B$ to the $-$ input, while the $+$ input is earthed at $0\text{ V}$. For an ideal op-amp, a positive $V_{IN}$ drives the output negative to keep the $-$ input at virtual earth.

Step 2: **Decide Voltmeter Polarity**
A voltmeter reads $V_{positive} - V_{negative}$. Here the op-amp output is negative, e.g. $-5.0\text{ V}$, while the other side of the meter is earth at $0\text{ V}$. To get a positive reading you need $$V = 0 - (-|V_{OUT}|) = +|V_{OUT}|$$ So P, the positive connection, must be the earthed lower lead between the earth symbol and the voltmeter.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: Calculate the potential $V_{IN}$ such that the voltmeter has a full-scale deflection when the inverting input to the op-amp is connected to
hints: Hint 1: Identify the type of amplifier gain involved here and notice which two resistor values control how large the output is compared to the input, and what output magnitude gives full-scale deflection.
Hint 2: Use the magnitude of the gain to work backwards from a $5.0\text{ V}$ magnitude output to the small $V_{IN}$ needed, checking $\text{k}\Omega$ to $\Omega$ conversion.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the Voltage Gain**
This is an inverting amplifier, so the magnitude of the voltage gain is set by feedback resistor over input resistor: $$|G| = \frac{R_F}{R_{IN}}$$ Here $R_F = 50\text{ k}\Omega = 50 \times 10^3\text{ }\Omega$ and $R_{IN} = R_A = 100\text{ }\Omega$. So $$|G| = \frac{50 \times 10^3}{100} = 500$$ The minus sign just means inversion.

Step 2: **Work Back From Full Scale**
Full-scale deflection means the meter magnitude is $5.0\text{ V}$, so $|V_{OUT}| = 5.0\text{ V}$. Since $|V_{OUT}| = |G| \times V_{IN}$: $$V_{IN} = \frac{|V_{OUT}|}{|G|} = \frac{5.0}{500} = 0.010\text{ V}$$ Only $10\text{ mV}$ at the input drives the output to full scale because the gain is so large.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: The circuit is the same except the input resistor is now much larger, so think about how that changes the size of the gain and therefore the larger input needed for the same $5.0\text{ V}$ output.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recalculate With $R_B$**
Now $R_{IN} = R_B = 10\text{ k}\Omega$ with the same $R_F = 50\text{ k}\Omega$. The gain magnitude is: $$|G| = \frac{R_F}{R_{IN}} = \frac{50\text{ k}\Omega}{10\text{ k}\Omega} = 5.0$$

Step 2: **Find New $V_{IN}$ For Full Scale**
Again $|V_{OUT}| = 5.0\text{ V}$ for full scale: $$V_{IN} = \frac{5.0}{5.0} = 1.0\text{ V}$$ A larger input resistor gives much smaller gain, so a much larger $1.0\text{ V}$ input is needed.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Suggest a use for this type of circuit.

markscheme_points.text: e.g. multi-range (volt)meter c.r.o. sensitivity control amplifier channel selector

hints: Hint 1: Look at what the switch does - it selects a different gain and a different full-scale input - so what measuring instrument would benefit from selectable sensitivity ranges?
parts.proper_answer: Use as a multi-range voltmeter (or voltage amplifier with selectable gain / sensitivity, e.g. input stage of a c.r.o.).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See The Purpose Of The Switch**
With $R_A$ the circuit measures up to about $0.010\text{ V}$ full scale, with $R_B$ it measures up to about $1.0\text{ V}$ full scale. The same $0-5.0\text{ V}$ meter can therefore cover very different input ranges just by switching the input resistor.

Step 2: **Name The Application**
That is exactly what a multi-range voltmeter does. It is an amplifier with switchable gain to allow small voltages to be measured with different sensitivities, also used as a sensitivity control or input selector for e.g. a c.r.o.
